common_name: Rosemary-Leaved Boxwood (Rosmarinifolia Narrow-Leaf English Boxwood)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Rosmarinifolia keeps its narrow foliage densest with some direct sun.

directions: Rosmarinifolia is an old, distinctive English boxwood form with narrow, gray-dusted green leaves so unlike typical boxwood foliage that it is easily mistaken for a dwarf conifer or an actual rosemary at a glance. It grows slowly into a dense, upright, fine-textured little shrub well suited to rock gardens, mixed borders, and small-scale topiary where its unusual texture stands out against broader-leaved neighbors. Once established it tolerates drought and lean soil better than many broader-leaved boxwood cultivars. Light annual shearing keeps the naturally tidy habit dense without erasing its wiry, needle-like character.

common_name: Grace Hendrick Phillips Boxwood (Ultra-Dwarf Mounding Littleleaf Boxwood)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained soil in partial shade in the Deep South or full sun in cooler climates; growth is extremely slow, so give plants time before judging spacing.

directions: Grace Hendrick Phillips is one of the slowest-growing littleleaf boxwood selections available, advancing only about an inch a year into a dense, low mound of small bright-green leaves that bronze lightly in winter sun. Its habit shifts with light exposure, staying low and spreading in full sun but becoming nearly conical in shade, which makes it a versatile choice for rock gardens, edging, and container or bonsai work where a true miniature scale matters. Because of its glacial growth rate it rarely needs shearing to stay in bounds. Good drainage is essential, and part shade suits it best in hot southern climates.

common_name: Golden Triumph Boxwood (Gold-Edged Compact Littleleaf Boxwood)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil with some direct sun to keep the gold leaf edges bright; too much shade fades the variegation toward plain green.

directions: Golden Triumph carries glossy, medium-to-large leaves edged in bright yellow that mellow to a soft bronze tint in cold weather, giving a warmer, showier look than the plain-green species. It grows slowly into a low, dense, rounded form that rarely exceeds a few feet even after a decade, making it easy to keep in scale in foundation plantings, low hedges, and mixed borders. Good drainage and at least a few hours of direct sun keep the variegation crisp through the growing season. Light shearing after the first spring flush maintains a tidy outline without cutting into the older, more richly colored wood.

common_name: Faulkner Boxwood (Compact Blue-Green Topiary Littleleaf Boxwood)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Faulkner tolerates more shade than many boxwood selections and holds a fine, dense habit well suited to shaping.

directions: Faulkner is a dense, slow-growing littleleaf boxwood prized for small, rounded, glossy blue-green leaves that turn a warm bronze in cold winter weather, then green back up in spring. Its naturally tight, uniform growth habit has long made it a favorite for globe and cone topiary as well as low formal hedging, since it holds a sheared shape with minimal regrowth between prunings. It has earned recognition from the Royal Horticultural Society for its reliable garden performance. Consistent moisture and part shade help it look its best through hot summers, and good air circulation reduces the leaf spot and blight pressure common to crowded boxwood plantings.

common_name: Twilight Witch Hazel (Yellow-to-Crimson Crimped-Petal Winter Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Twilight grows into a larger, more vigorous plant than most hybrid witch hazels, so allow generous room.

directions: Twilight is an unusually vigorous hybrid witch hazel that can reach well over ten feet, considerably larger than most named intermedia cultivars, with a rounded, spreading crown. Its curiously crimped, spidery petals open across a wide color range on the same plant, with some clusters cheerful yellow, others deep crimson, and many flowers a streaked mix of the two, giving each specimen an individual look. Bloom occurs on bare wood in late winter, well ahead of most spring-flowering shrubs, and light fall color follows the foliage before it drops. Give it plenty of open space rather than a tight foundation planting so its naturally large, informal form can develop.

common_name: Candlelight Vigil Witch Hazel (Fragrant Yellow Late-Winter Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Candlelight Vigil blooms later than many hybrid witch hazels, extending the winter display.

directions: Candlelight Vigil is a lesser-known hybrid witch hazel selected by breeder Tim Brotzman, valued for clear yellow, strongly fragrant flowers that open in late winter after many earlier-blooming cultivars have already finished. Its later flowering window helps stretch the witch hazel season into early spring in gardens that also grow earlier orange- and red-flowered selections. Plants develop the same vase-shaped, multi-stemmed habit typical of the group, with clean green summer foliage and yellow fall color. Underplant with early bulbs or hellebores to echo its late-winter bloom time.

common_name: Orange Encore Witch Hazel (Late-Blooming Fragrant Orange Winter Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Orange Encore flowers later than most hybrid witch hazels, often as new leaves begin to emerge.

directions: Orange Encore lives up to its name by extending the witch hazel bloom season, unfurling frilly, fragrant orange-yellow flowers in late winter to very early spring, later than the bulk of the popular intermedia cultivars. Emerging spring foliage carries a distinctive maroon-red tint before settling into green for summer, then returns to a showy crimson in fall, giving it strong multi-season interest beyond the flowers alone. Its rounded, vase-shaped habit fits well at the back of a shrub border or as a specimen near a path where the late-season color can be enjoyed up close. Prune immediately after flowering if size control is needed, since next year's buds form quickly afterward.

common_name: Brimstone Witch Hazel (Narrow Upright Bright-Yellow Purple-Centered Winter Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Brimstone's narrow, upright habit fits tighter spaces than many spreading hybrid witch hazels.

directions: Brimstone stands apart from most hybrid witch hazels with an unusually narrow, upright silhouette and extraordinarily bright yellow flowers marked with nearly purple-black centers, creating a striking contrast during the bleakest weeks of midwinter. Its more columnar shape makes it easier to fit into narrower side yards or tighter shrub borders than the typically wide-spreading intermedia cultivars. Clean green summer foliage turns yellow in fall before the bare winter framework takes over the display. Full sun brings out the deepest flower color and keeps the habit dense and upright rather than open.

common_name: Double Gold Witch Hazel (Variegated Gold-Margined Sport of Westerstede)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; some direct sun keeps the variegated leaf margins bright on Double Gold.

directions: Double Gold arose as a branch sport on the popular pale-yellow cultivar 'Westerstede' discovered in the Netherlands, and it is grown as much for its variegated foliage as for its flowers. New spring leaves emerge with a bright yellow margin that fades to a softer creamy yellow edge as the season progresses, giving the shrub season-long interest well beyond the typical witch hazel bloom window. In late winter it also carries medium yellow, stiff-petaled, faintly scented flowers on bare wood like its parent cultivar. Give it a site with some direct sun, since deeper shade dulls both the variegation and the density of flowering.

common_name: Burning Desire Witch Hazel (Deep Orange Crimped-Petal Winter Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Burning Desire forms a broad, rounded shrub about as wide as tall at maturity.

directions: Burning Desire is a more recent orange-flowered selection from English witch hazel authority Chris Lane, bearing clusters of lightly scented, deep orange, crimped-petal flowers on bare branches through the winter months. It develops into a rounded, deciduous shrub of roughly equal height and spread, with broadly oval leaves that turn attractive shades of yellow and orange in autumn before the winter flower display begins. Its saturated orange flower color reads as deeper and warmer than many older orange cultivars, making it a strong choice for gardeners wanting to build a color gradient of witch hazels from pale yellow through red. Full sun produces the most flowers and the richest fall foliage color.

common_name: Strawberries and Cream Witch Hazel (Pale Yellow and Red Bicolor Winter Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Strawberries and Cream keeps a neatly rounded habit that needs little corrective pruning.

directions: Strawberries and Cream produces an unusual bicolor flower, with pale creamy-yellow petals splashed and streaked with red toward the base, said to resemble strawberries dusted with cream from a short distance. The flowers open on bare stems in late winter with the light spicy fragrance typical of hybrid witch hazels, and the neatly rounded shrub carries clean green summer foliage that turns gold in fall. Its more compact, evenly proportioned habit makes it easier to place in a foundation planting or smaller garden than some of the larger-growing intermedia cultivars. Full sun to light shade in moist, well-drained soil keeps flowering dense from year to year.

common_name: Gay Sue Camellia (Fragrant Double White Sasanqua)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to filtered sun; Gay Sue grows a bit faster than many sasanqua cultivars and benefits from being sited with room to spread.

directions: Gay Sue is a New Zealand-raised sasanqua seedling prized for its frilled, peony-form white flowers with a distinct musky fragrance, opening from pink-tipped buds from early autumn into early winter. Plants grow upright and reasonably vigorous, with light green foliage that shows off the pale flowers clearly against the darker green of most other camellias nearby. Acidic, humus-rich soil with reliable moisture and dappled shade produces the strongest bloom and the glossiest foliage. Its scent makes it a good choice near a path, porch, or window where the fragrance can be appreciated on cool fall mornings.

common_name: Hinode-gumo Camellia (Sunrise Cloud Blush-Edged White Sasanqua)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to filtered sun; Hinode-gumo is vigorous and upright enough to train as a hedge, screen, or espalier.

directions: Hinode-gumo, whose Japanese name translates roughly to Sunrise Cloud, is a long-cultivated sasanqua dating to 1938 valued for large, semi-double white flowers with a delicate blush-pink edge along the petals. It is one of the more vigorous, upright-growing sasanqua selections, capable of reaching well over head height and holding up well as a clipped hedge, screen, or wall-trained espalier. Flowering is late in the sasanqua season, typically running from November into December, with new blooms opening in succession over several weeks. Provide the same acidic, well-drained, humus-rich conditions favored by other camellias, with morning sun and afternoon shade in hot climates.

common_name: Little Pearl Camellia (Compact Double Blush-White Shishi-Form Sasanqua)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Little Pearl's compact size and dense habit suit large containers as well as in-ground planting.

directions: Little Pearl, bred by Nuccio's Nurseries in California, produces small, layered, double 'shishi'-form flowers that open from pink buds to a soft blush-white with a faint pink wash along the petal edges and backs. Its small, glossy dark-green leaves and compact, upright habit stay proportionally smaller than many sasanqua cultivars, making it a good fit for screens, hedges, espaliers, or large containers where a full-sized camellia would overwhelm the space. Bloom runs through late autumn into early winter with abundant, fragrant flowers held close against the foliage. Consistent moisture and acidic, well-drained soil with dappled shade keep the compact form dense and free-flowering.

common_name: Beatrice Emily Camellia (Large Double White Pink-Edged Sasanqua)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Beatrice Emily tolerates more sun than many sasanqua cultivars and flowers heavily as a result.

directions: Beatrice Emily is an Australian-raised sasanqua noted for an abundance of large, fully double white flowers with soft pink-tinged outer petals, carrying the earthy, faintly sweet fragrance typical of the group. Plants grow into a dense, upright, well-branched shrub with shiny deep-green foliage, reaching substantial size over time and taking well to shearing as a hedge, screen, or espalier. It flowers heavily through autumn into early winter and tolerates more direct sun than many sasanqua selections, which helps drive the heavy bud set. Regular moisture and acidic, well-drained soil keep the glossy foliage dense from the ground up.

common_name: Paradise Diana Camellia (Vigorous Large Single Pink Sasanqua)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Paradise Diana grows quickly into a large shrub or small tree, so allow generous space or plant it as a screen.

directions: Paradise Diana, part of the Australian-bred Paradise series of sasanqua camellias, produces very large single soft-pink flowers centered with prominent bright yellow stamens from early autumn through winter. It is one of the faster, more vigorous growers in the group, developing an upright, long-lived habit that can be trained into a small tree or kept as a tall informal hedge or screen. Like other Paradise selections it tolerates more heat, sun, and light frost than many older sasanqua cultivars, making it useful for exposed sites. Consistent moisture and acidic, well-drained soil support its rapid growth and heavy autumn bloom.

common_name: Paradise Exotic Jewel Camellia (Deep Pink Aging to Crimson Double Sasanqua)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to filtered sun; Paradise Exotic Jewel holds an elegant, slightly arching, upright habit that needs little corrective pruning.

directions: Paradise Exotic Jewel is a mid-season member of the Paradise sasanqua series, opening double flowers in a glowing deep pink that gradually ages to a rich crimson-red as blooms mature on the shrub. Clusters of lightly perfumed flowers appear from around May in its native Southern Hemisphere season, translating to a late-fall to early-winter display in most of the United States. Its elegant, slightly arching, upright form and deep green foliage give it good structure even out of bloom, and it takes well to light shaping as a specimen or informal hedge. Acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil and dappled shade produce the richest flower color.

common_name: Paradise Helen Camellia (Pink-Budded Double White Compact Sasanqua)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Paradise Helen tolerates more sun than many sasanqua cultivars and flowers densely as a low hedge.

directions: Paradise Helen opens masses of bright pink buds that unfurl to dazzling white, informal double flowers with a soft pink wash and golden-yellow anthers at the center, set against glossy dark-green, finely serrated foliage. Its compact, upright, free-flowering habit and good sun tolerance make it a popular choice for low, dense hedging and mass plantings where a long autumn-into-winter bloom display is wanted. It is a long-lived, hardy shrub that recovers well from shearing, holding its shape through repeated seasonal pruning. Regular moisture and acidic, well-drained soil keep flower production heavy year after year.

common_name: Paradise Little Liane Camellia (Slow-Growing Compact White Small-Leaf Sasanqua)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Paradise Little Liane's slow, compact growth suits topiary, low borders, and containers better than full-sized sasanqua.

directions: Paradise Little Liane, also sold as Paradise Petite Little Liane, is a small-leaved, slow-growing, distinctly compact sasanqua bred at Paradise Plants Nursery in Australia, producing semi-double to informal double white flowers in proportion to its miniature scale. Its dense, fine-textured habit and naturally restrained size make it well suited to low borders, topiary, and long-term container culture, roles that would quickly outgrow a standard full-sized sasanqua. Flowering follows the typical autumn-to-winter sasanqua pattern, with clean white blooms held close against small, glossy foliage. Acidic, well-drained soil with steady moisture and light shade keep growth dense without pushing it beyond its compact habit.

common_name: Little Heath Green Pieris (All-Green Reversion of Little Heath Andromeda)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Little Heath Green keeps the same dwarf, compact habit as variegated Little Heath without the cream leaf margins.

directions: Little Heath Green is the plain-green counterpart of the popular variegated dwarf 'Little Heath,' arising as a reversion selection that keeps the same compact, dense, slow-growing mound but without the cream-white leaf margins. New spring growth still emerges with a bright scarlet flush before settling into glossy dark green, and small clusters of white, urn-shaped flowers appear in early spring. Its true-dwarf size makes it useful for foundation plantings, rock gardens, and small borders where the larger species would quickly outgrow the space. Consistent moisture in acidic, well-drained soil and shelter from harsh winter wind keep the compact form looking its best.

common_name: Pink Delight Pieris (Late-Blooming Fading Pink Andromeda, AGM)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Pink Delight breaks growth and flowers later than most cultivars, which helps it dodge late spring frosts.

directions: Pink Delight is a bushy, medium-sized andromeda that flowers freely even while young, producing large drooping panicles of pink buds that open pink and gradually fade to blush white. It holds the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit for reliable garden performance, and its new bronze-tinted foliage matures to a clean dark green through the growing season. Because it comes into growth and bloom three to four weeks later than many pieris cultivars, it usually escapes the late frosts that can blacken the buds and new leaves of earlier-flowering selections. Give it acidic, humus-rich, evenly moist soil in partial shade and shelter from harsh winter sun and wind.

common_name: Pink Passion Pieris (Fragrant Pale Pink Long-Panicled Andromeda)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Pink Passion carries long flower panicles best displayed where the plant can be viewed from below or at eye level.

directions: Pink Passion is an upright, bushy andromeda selected for long, lightly fragrant panicles of pale pink, urn-shaped flowers carried over an extended spring bloom period. Glossy, oblong to lance-shaped dark-green leaves provide a clean evergreen backdrop to the drooping flower clusters, and the plant builds a well-proportioned, somewhat taller habit than many of the true-dwarf pieris cultivars. It performs best with the same acidic, humus-rich, consistently moist soil that all Japanese andromeda selections require, sited in partial shade with protection from harsh winter sun and wind. Mulching to keep the shallow root zone cool and moist helps it establish and bloom reliably.

common_name: Grayswood Pieris (Historic Tall Yellow-Margined Variegated Andromeda)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Grayswood grows considerably taller over time than most compact modern pieris cultivars, so give it room.

directions: Grayswood is a historic English selection named for Grayswood Hill in Surrey, where an old specimen grew to around twelve feet, making it one of the taller-growing named pieris cultivars available. Its narrower-than-typical leaves are edged in yellowish white, giving a more refined variegated texture than the broader, bolder patterning of cultivars like 'Variegata' or 'Flaming Silver'. Clusters of small white, urn-shaped flowers appear in spring against the variegated foliage, and the shrub's eventual size suits it to a specimen role or the back of a shaded shrub border rather than a tight foundation planting. Consistent moisture in acidic, humus-rich soil and shelter from harsh winter wind and sun help prevent leaf scorch on the pale leaf margins.

common_name: Wada's Pink Pieris (Deep Pink Bud Clear-Pink Flowered Andromeda)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Wada's Pink holds a compact, rounded habit well suited to a shrub border or mass planting.

directions: Wada's Pink is a garden-origin pieris selection carrying deep pink flower buds that open to clear, unfading pink, urn-shaped blooms in April, offering a stronger, more saturated pink than many of the older pink-flowered andromeda selections. It builds into a compact, well-rounded shrub reaching around four feet, making a good specimen for a shaded border or grouped for a mass planting near other acid-loving companions like rhododendrons and azaleas. Glossy evergreen foliage provides year-round structure, with a light bronze new-growth flush in spring. As with all pieris, acidic, humus-rich, evenly moist soil and shelter from drying winter wind keep the foliage and flower buds from browning.
